title: The Price of a Falling Rupee
problem: Between 2015 and 2025, food prices in Pakistan nearly tripled. Over the same period the rupee lost much of its value against the US dollar, while world food prices rose only a little. We want to know whether the weak rupee is the main reason food became so expensive.
question: Do a weaker rupee, world food prices and fuel costs raise food prices in Pakistan — and do food prices fall back when the rupee gets stronger?

variables.name: Food Prices
variables.why: What families pay for food — the thing we want to explain.

variables.name: Dollar Rate
variables.measure: Rupees needed to buy 1 US dollar (monthly average)
variables.why: A higher number = a weaker rupee, so imports cost more.

variables.name: World Food Prices
variables.why: Prices of wheat, oil, sugar, dairy and meat on world markets.

variables.name: Fuel & Transport Costs
variables.measure: Transport price index, mostly petrol & diesel (2015-16 = 100)
variables.why: Fuel is needed to grow food and move it to the market.

equation_general: Food Prices = β₀ + β₁ Dollar Rate + β₂ World Food Prices + β₃ Fuel & Transport Costs + error
equation_estimated: Food Prices = -2.22 + 0.64 × Dollar Rate + 0.61 × World Food Prices + 0.21 × Fuel & Transport Costs
equation_note: All variables are in logarithms, so each number is an elasticity: the % change in food prices for a 1% change in that variable. Estimated with an ARDL model (long-run form) on monthly data, 2015–2025.

coefficients.name: Dollar Rate
coefficients.plain: A 10% rise in Dollar Rate → food prices about 6.3% higher in the long run.

coefficients.name: World Food Prices
coefficients.plain: A 10% rise in World Food Prices → food prices about 5.9% higher in the long run.

coefficients.name: Fuel & Transport Costs
coefficients.plain: Its effect (0.21) is too uncertain to be distinguished from zero (p = 0.36).

hypotheses.question: Does a weaker rupee raise food prices?
hypotheses.h0: The dollar rate has no effect on food prices (β₁ = 0).
hypotheses.h1: A higher dollar rate raises food prices (β₁ ≠ 0).

hypotheses.question: Do world food prices raise Pakistan's food prices?
hypotheses.h0: World food prices have no effect (β₂ = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Higher world food prices raise food prices (β₂ ≠ 0).

hypotheses.question: Do fuel & transport costs raise food prices?
hypotheses.h0: Fuel & transport costs have no effect (β₃ = 0).
hypotheses.h1: Higher fuel & transport costs raise food prices (β₃ ≠ 0).

hypotheses.question: Do these variables move together in the long run?
Does a falling rupee and a rising rupee affect food prices equally?
hypotheses.h0: The effect of a falling rupee equals the effect of a rising rupee (symmetry).
hypotheses.result: Short run: p = 0.023 → different. Long run: p = 0.495 → cannot say they differ.
hypotheses.decision: Reject H0 in the short run · Fail to reject H0 in the long run

tests.name: Descriptive Statistics
tests.checks: Average, spread, lowest and highest value of each variable.
tests.result: Food prices rose 194.0%, the dollar rate 178.0%, world food prices 23.0%.
tests.meaning: Pakistan's food prices rose far more than world food prices.

tests.name: Correlation Matrix
tests.checks: How strongly each pair of variables moves together (−1 to +1).
tests.result: Food Prices vs Dollar Rate: r = 0.98; vs World Food Prices: r = 0.79.
tests.meaning: Food prices and the dollar rate move together very closely.

tests.name: ADF Unit Root Test
tests.checks: Whether each series has a stable average (stationary) or keeps trending.
tests.h0: The series has a unit root (not stationary).
tests.result: All four: not stationary in levels, stationary after first difference → I(1).
tests.meaning: The data trend over time, so plain OLS could mislead — we use ARDL, which handles this.

tests.name: ARDL Bounds Test
tests.checks: Whether the variables share a long-run relationship.
tests.meaning: Food prices, the dollar rate and world food prices are tied together in the long run.

tests.name: Error Correction (ECM)
tests.checks: How fast food prices return to the long-run path after a shock.
tests.meaning: About 12% of any gap closes every month; half of it is gone in about 5.4 months.

tests.name: Wald Test (Asymmetry)
tests.checks: Whether a falling and a rising rupee have the same effect.
tests.result: Short run p = 0.023; long run p = 0.495
tests.decision: Short run: reject · Long run: fail to reject
tests.meaning: When the rupee recovers, food prices do not come down in the same month.

tests.name: Breusch-Godfrey (Serial Correlation)
tests.checks: Whether errors from one month repeat in the next.
tests.meaning: No leftover pattern in the errors — good.

tests.name: Breusch-Pagan-Godfrey (Heteroskedasticity)
tests.checks: Whether the size of errors changes with the variables.

tests.name: Jarque-Bera (Normality)
tests.checks: Whether the errors follow a normal (bell-shaped) distribution.
tests.meaning: A few extreme months (e.g. May 2024) make errors non-normal. With 128 months this does not change the conclusions.

tests.name: Ramsey RESET (Model Form)
tests.checks: Whether the equation's shape is correct.
tests.meaning: The equation's form is fine — good.

tests.name: CUSUM & CUSUM of Squares (Stability)
tests.checks: Whether the relationship stayed stable over 2015–2025.
tests.result: CUSUM inside 5% bands; CUSUMSQ inside 5% bands
tests.meaning: The relationship held steady over the whole period — good.

answer: YES — a weaker rupee raises food prices. A 10% rise in the dollar rate goes with about 6.3% higher food prices in the long run.
YES — world food prices matter too: a 10% rise goes with about 5.9% higher food prices.
NOT CLEAR — fuel & transport costs: the effect is positive but not statistically significant.
When the rupee gets stronger, food prices do NOT fall in the same month. Over the long run we cannot prove the fall is smaller — there were too few months of a rising rupee to tell.
one_line: The rupee's fall is paid for at the market: when the rupee weakens, food gets dearer — and it does not get cheaper again quickly when the rupee recovers.
